question: The randomized-look policy passes every check and succeeds in the simulator. On the real arm it runs the whole plan and closes its jaws beside the cube. Is the miss caused by where the cube is, by the camera, or by the joint map?
measure: Where the cube really is, in mm on the table, read from the real start frame through the calibrated lens (back-projection), against the pose the task assumes. And for each live attempt: how many steps ran, what stopped it, and how far the gripper closed (about 0.5 units means it closed on nothing).
outcome: Placement. The cube sat about 40 mm farther from the base and 11 mm to the side of the task pose; training covered plus or minus 10 mm. A second problem: a strict safety rule froze the arm when the servo lagged. Both were fixed. No grasp yet.
setup:
A policy is the network that drives the arm. Ours looks at the wrist camera image and the joint angles and outputs the next 90 joint commands at once. Those 90 commands are a chunk. A new chunk is made at steps 0, 90, 180 and so on. An episode is 480 steps at 30 Hz, about 16 seconds. The policy here is the randomized-look one from experiment 25. It only trained with the cube within plus or minus 10 mm of one spot: the centre of a square 8.5 inches from the front edge of the arm's base.

Back-projection means taking a pixel in the camera image and working out which point on the table it shows, using the calibrated lens model and the camera's pose. The joint map converts servo readings into joint angles.

The runner's safety gate checks every command. One rule, the relative limit, refuses a command that is more than 20 units ahead of where the servo is. Until this experiment a refused command meant a hold: the arm stays put for that step, and 15 holds in a row abort the run. The real-frame gate (experiment 25) checks that the first chunk on a real start frame holds still.

parts.conclusion: In attempt 9 the lift chunk climbed about 4 units per step and the servo lagged. Once the gap passed the 20-unit relative limit, the hold rule froze the arm while the chunk's targets kept moving on, so the abort was certain. Fix: on a relative-limit-only violation, send the rate-limited command and continue. Range and floor limits still hold. The simulator never triggers this limit, so scored rollouts do not change.

The record says 20 to 40 mm off. The sources give 40 mm (attempt 4) and readings of 46, 18, 25 and 19 mm on later attempts

meaning: Two things stood between the policy and a real grasp, and neither was the network. The bench was set up with the towel's near edge where its centre should be, and the hold-on-any-violation rule could not work with real motor lag. With the cube re-placed, the tolerance widened to 35 mm and the gate changed to rate-limit and continue, the next attempt (experiment 27) succeeded.
lesson: When a real run fails, measure the world before blaming the model. And test your safety rules against real motor lag: a rule that never fires in the simulator can make a real run impossible.

log:
**TL;DR:** The plan ran fine but the jaws closed beside the cube, because the
cube sat 20-40 mm off from where the task assumed, and a strict safety rule kept
freezing the arm.

**Problem.** The randomized-look policy ran on the real arm and missed.

*How we know:* attempt 4 ran 427 steps at 30 Hz with no timing misses, and the
gripper closed on nothing. The same policy in sim succeeds.

**Experiment.** Map the real start frame onto the table through the calibrated
lens (back-projection) to measure where the cube actually was. Then refuse to
run unless the cube is close enough, and print how to move it.

*What we hope to learn:* whether the miss is the cube's placement, the camera,
or the joint map.

**Outcome.** The towel's near edge was right where the square's centre should
be, so the cube was about 40 mm farther than intended and 11 mm to the side.
Training only covered ±10 mm. Attempt 5 failed the real-frame check (the cube had
been knocked off the towel), and the new placement check refused 6-8 (46, 18
and 25 mm off). Attempt 9 ran, but the lift outran the servo:

- The safety rule froze the arm whenever a command jumped too far ahead of the
  servo, while the plan kept moving on. Like a driver who brakes every time the
  car lags the pedal. Fix: on a speed-only violation, send the speed-limited
  command and keep going. Range limits still stop it.

Later I found the cube reading shifts by about 25 mm with the arm's pose, so the
40 mm isn't exact.

**Takeaway:** when a real run fails, measure the world before blaming the model,
and test your safety rules against real motor lag.
